questions.q: Why can a test with zero assertions still show 100% line coverage of the function it calls?
options: Because Forge automatically adds assertions
Because coverage only tracks whether a line executed, not whether anything about its result was checked
Because 100% coverage is impossible without assertions
Because Forge ignores functions with no assertions
questions.explain: The lesson's key point: coverage answers "did this line run," not "was the result correct" — a test can execute every line and assert nothing.

questions.q: What does Foundry's `vm.expectRevert` cheatcode do?
options: It skips the next test if it would revert
It asserts that the next call reverts, optionally with a specific error or message
It forces a contract to always revert
It measures the gas cost of a reverted call
questions.explain: `vm.expectRevert` is how you assert a failure path actually fails, instead of only testing success paths.

questions.q: What does `forge snapshot` produce?
options: A screenshot of the terminal
A .gas-snapshot file recording every test's gas usage as a committed baseline
A deployment transaction
A list of all contract addresses
questions.explain: forge snapshot runs the test suite and writes each test's gas usage into .gas-snapshot, which gets committed as the baseline to compare future runs against.

questions.q: What does `targetContract()` do in an invariant test?
options: Deploys the contract to mainnet
Tells Forge which contract's public functions to generate a random call sequence against
Marks a contract as immutable
Deletes the contract after the test
questions.explain: targetContract() designates which contract Forge fuzzes a sequence of calls against, checking the invariant after each call.

questions.q: What is the single fact that most fundamentally distinguishes smart contract CI/CD from web app CI/CD, per this lesson?
options: Smart contracts can't be tested automatically
Deployed contract bytecode is (without a proxy) immutable — there's no hotfix or rollback once it's live
Smart contracts don't need a build step
Web apps never need static analysis
questions.explain: Once CREATE/CREATE2 puts bytecode on-chain, it's permanent — unlike a web app, there's no quick hotfix or revert for a live contract without a proxy pattern.

questions.q: By default, what happens if a GitHub Actions status check on a PR fails, but no branch protection rule marks it as required?
options: The merge button is automatically disabled
The repository is automatically archived
The PR can still be merged — a non-required check is purely informational
GitHub emails the repo owner every hour
questions.explain: A status check that isn't marked required in a branch protection rule doesn't block anything — it's just a visible signal a reviewer can ignore.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a linter and a static analyzer, per this lesson?
options: They are the same tool with different names
A linter checks style/convention; a static analyzer reasons about control/data flow to flag vulnerability patterns
A linter only works on Hardhat projects, a static analyzer only on Foundry
A static analyzer executes the code; a linter never reads the code at all
questions.explain: A linter cares about how code is written (formatting, naming); a static analyzer reasons about what the code does, without executing it, to flag risky patterns.

questions.q: Why does `submodules: recursive` matter specifically for a Foundry project's checkout step?
options: It's required by all GitHub Actions workflows regardless of language
Foundry dependencies like OpenZeppelin and forge-std are usually installed as git submodules, not via an npm-style package manager
It speeds up the Solidity compiler
It's only needed for Hardhat projects, not Foundry
questions.explain: Without recursive submodule checkout, the build fails on missing imports, since Foundry projects typically manage dependencies as git submodules.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend `--account` (a keystore account) over a raw `--private-key` flag?
options: Because --private-key is deprecated and no longer works
Because a raw private key in a flag puts a plaintext key into shell history and process arguments — a keystore keeps it encrypted on disk
Because --account is faster to type
Because --private-key only works on testnets
questions.explain: --account uses an encrypted keystore, prompting for a password only at broadcast time, instead of exposing a plaintext key in shell history.

questions.q: How does the lesson describe wiring a Safe into a deployment pipeline?
options: The deploy script broadcasts directly with no human involvement, same as a single-key deploy
A deploy/upgrade transaction is proposed to the Safe, then the required number of owners confirm it through Safe{Wallet} before it executes on-chain
Every team member must independently redeploy the same contract
Safe cannot be used for contract deployments, only for token transfers
questions.explain: The lesson describes a propose-then-confirm flow: a transaction is proposed to the Safe (e.g. by CI), and enough owners must confirm it before it actually executes.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT something a testnet deployment can be relied on to validate, per this lesson?
options: Whether the deploy script's constructor arguments are correct
Whether the contract's bytecode fits under the size limit
Whether the contract is safe under real mainnet liquidity depth and MEV pressure
Whether basic integration with testnet infrastructure behaves as expected
questions.explain: Real liquidity depth and MEV pressure don't exist on a testnet — those are exactly the economic conditions a testnet deployment can't validate.

questions.q: What becomes available on a contract's explorer page only after verification succeeds?
options: The ability to deploy a new version
The Read Contract and Write Contract tabs, plus decoded function calls and events instead of raw hex
A lower gas price for future transactions
Automatic bug bounty enrollment
questions.explain: Before verification, a contract is opaque bytecode; after a successful match, the explorer unlocks Read/Write tabs and decodes calls and events using the published ABI.

questions.q: When is an archive node required instead of a full node?
options: For fork testing at a specific historical block (Chapter 1, Lesson 4) or backfilling an indexer against old events
An archive node is never actually needed for any blockchain task
Only when sending brand-new transactions, never for reads
Full nodes and archive nodes provide identical data in all cases
questions.explain: A full node only holds recent state; historical state back to genesis requires an archive node, which fork testing and event backfilling both depend on.

questions.q: How does a CI platform's secret store keep a value like DEPLOYER_PRIVATE_KEY out of the workflow file and commit history?
options: The value is set once in the platform's settings and injected as an environment variable only at run time, referenced by name in the workflow
The value is written directly into the YAML workflow file and relies on the repo being private
CI platforms do not support secrets at all -- values must be hardcoded
The secret is emailed to the deployer manually before each run
questions.explain: This extends the GitHub Actions pattern from Chapter 2, Lesson 8: secrets are referenced by name and injected at run time, never appearing in the workflow file itself.

questions.q: Why pull a specific, pinned, published base image instead of hand-building one or floating on a tag like 'latest'?
options: The same reproducibility argument as pinning a Solidity compiler version -- an unpinned base image means the build isn't reproducible
Pinned images cannot contain any vulnerabilities
Floating tags like 'latest' are required by Docker and cannot be avoided
Pinning a base image version removes the need to ever scan it
questions.explain: A pinned, published image is reproducible the same way a pinned compiler version is -- 'it worked on my machine' becomes a checkable fact, not a guess.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of an automatic preview deployment for every pull request?
options: A reviewer can connect a test wallet and click through the actual proposed UI before it ever reaches production
It replaces the need for a production deployment entirely
It automatically audits the smart contract the frontend calls
It only shows a static screenshot of the proposed change, not a running app
questions.explain: A live preview URL lets a reviewer interact with the real running UI -- important when a frontend bug could mean a user signs the wrong transaction.

questions.q: How does alerting differ from the dashboard-based monitoring covered in Lesson 22?
options: An alert condition is evaluated continuously and fires automatically, instead of requiring a human to be actively watching a dashboard
Alerting replaces the need for any dashboard or monitoring numbers
Alerting only works if someone manually refreshes a page every minute
Alerting and dashboard monitoring are identical in every respect
questions.explain: Dashboards require someone to be looking at the right moment; alerting removes that dependency by firing automatically when a condition is true.

questions.q: What does 'price deviation' as a monitoring signal refer to?
options: A pool pricing an asset meaningfully away from the rest of the market, which can signal manipulation or a broken oracle
The gas price paid for a single transaction
The difference between a contract's bytecode and its verified source
A scheduled, expected daily price update
questions.explain: When a pool's price diverges significantly from the broader market's price for the same asset, it's a red flag worth investigating.

questions.q: Why does acknowledging an incident immediately matter, even before the cause is known?
options: Silence in the first hour reads as denial or indifference, even if the team is actively investigating
Acknowledging immediately is legally required in every jurisdiction
It has no effect on user trust either way
It allows the team to skip writing a postmortem later
questions.explain: Users watching a protocol's channels interpret silence negatively; a prompt acknowledgment signals the team is aware and working the problem.

questions.q: Why should alerts route to different destinations based on severity, rather than all going to the same place?
options: A routine check-in can go to email, while something needing an immediate human response needs to reach PagerDuty or an on-call rotation
All alerts should always go to the same destination regardless of urgency
Severity-based routing is only relevant for smart contract testing, not incident response
Email is always the correct destination for every kind of alert
questions.explain: Routing based on severity ensures urgent incidents reach someone who can respond immediately, while routine signals don't create unnecessary urgency.

questions.q: What should actually trigger raising a deposit cap, according to this lesson?
options: Evidence that real usage has run cleanly with no incidents -- not simply the passage of a fixed amount of calendar time
A fixed two-week countdown that applies regardless of actual usage
A single engineer's decision made independently of any approval process
The cap should never be raised under any circumstances
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly argues for raising caps based on evidence of clean real-world usage, not a calendar schedule.

questions.q: What course does this lesson name as the next and final course in the Blockchain Engineer path?
options: Blockchain Engineering Capstones
Blockchain Development
A repeat of this same course from Lesson 1
There is no further course in the path
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly names Blockchain Engineering Capstones as the final course, where everything from this course and earlier ones comes together in end-to-end projects.

questions.q: What is the key structural difference between a security audit and a bug bounty program?
options: An audit is a fixed-duration engagement that ends with a report, while a bug bounty is an open-ended program that runs indefinitely after launch
They are functionally identical and interchangeable in every respect
A bug bounty always happens before launch, and an audit always happens after
An audit never produces a report, only a bug bounty does
questions.explain: An audit is time-boxed and concludes with a report; a bug bounty has no fixed end date and keeps running as long as the protocol is live.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend actually triggering the pause mechanism before launch, rather than just confirming it exists in the code?
options: So the people who'd need to use it during a real incident have already practiced doing so, rather than using it for the first time under pressure
Triggering it before launch permanently disables the mechanism for later use
Pause mechanisms cannot be tested without affecting real user funds
It has no practical benefit over simply reading the contract's pause function
questions.explain: A rehearsed pause means the relevant people already know how to use it, rather than discovering how it works for the first time during an actual incident.
